title: CV formats for Swiss employers vs ATS bots — what actually gets past both?
body: I'm finishing my bachelor at Les Roches and starting to apply for entry roles at Swiss hotels. Everyone gives me different advice: one career counsellor says Swiss HR managers expect a photo, DOB and nationality on the CV, while another says those exact fields trip up ATS scanners. I've also heard Swiss recruiters hate the Europass template and want a standard one-page CV with a cover letter in German or French. On top of that, some big-chain portals only accept .docx, which breaks my nice PDF layout. I'd love to know what's actually been working for people here. Questions: do you include a photo and personal details or skip them? One page or two for a new grad? And is the cover letter a dealbreaker in the local language even if my German is only B1? Has anyone tested applying through ATS-heavy portals vs sending a direct email to HR?

title: Is LinkedIn Premium actually worth it for a fresh hospitality grad, or a waste of money?
body: I keep getting the 'one month free' LinkedIn Premium offers right after graduation and I'm genuinely torn. The InMail credits sound useful for reaching hotel HR directors and F&B managers directly, but I've read that most recruiters reply to normal connection requests anyway, so InMail might be a gimmick. The 'who viewed your profile' feature is tempting for a job hunt, but realistically I probably get five views a day. What I'd actually use it for is seeing whether recruiters search for hospitality grads and boosting my open-to-work visibility. Questions: has Premium actually gotten anyone here an interview, or is the money better spent on a CV service or a hotel certification? Does having Premium make you look desperate to recruiters, or does nobody care? And do the bounties/free trials actually expire cleanly, or is it a pain to cancel before the charge?

title: 5-star management trainee programmes — how realistic is landing one straight out of school?
body: I'm at EHL and everyone around me is either applying to MT programmes or acting like they're guaranteed if you just graduate. I've been looking at the big ones — Fairmont, Four Seasons, Ritz-Carlton, Kempinski — and most ask for 6-12 months of operational experience before you even apply, which feels circular when you've just come out of school. Some friends say MT programmes are basically cheap F&B labour rotations where the manager title never materialises, while others claim they're the only real route to a DOSM or GM role. Questions: what does the selection process actually weigh — internship track record, on-campus grades, or the panel interview? Is it better to apply through the group's careers portal months in advance, or to reach out to a specific hotel's HRD after a short internship? And how do you spot an MT that actually leads to a management role versus one that just fills shifts?

title: First offer in Switzerland — can you negotiate, and what's take-home after Quellensteuer?
body: I just got my first offer from a hotel near Lausanne (SHMS grad here) and I'm a bit lost. The gross is 4,200 CHF/month with the 13th salary included, but I genuinely can't figure out what the net will be once Quellensteuer is deducted at source — every calculator I try gives me a different number. My family back home keeps telling me to negotiate, but everyone I've asked at the hotel says first offers in Switzerland are usually take-it-or-leave-it for junior roles, and I don't want to look difficult before I even start. Questions: how realistic is pushing back on a standard first offer, and is it smarter to ask for better accommodation or meal perks instead of a higher base? Is 4,200 with the 13th roughly the norm for a first F&B position around Lac Léman? And for anyone already on Quellensteuer — is net pay lower in the first months because of B permit withholding, or does it level out?

title: Is EHL's bachelor really as brutal as people say, or is it survivable with planning?
body: Starting my first semester at EHL in September and the secondhand stories are doing my head in. People talk about the first year being all operations — working the mock-hotel environments like La Ruche, endless group projects — while simultaneously grinding through core business modules. Some alumni say the busy semesters are a marathon with no social life; others say it's only the group dynamics that are painful and that solo work is fine. I'm trying to set realistic expectations before I arrive. Questions: roughly how many hours a week do people actually put in during the heavy semesters, and is the group project load genuinely as bad as claimed? Is it realistic to hold a part-time job or do a meaningful extracurricular during term, or is that a mistake in year one? And do semesters alternate between light and heavy so you can plan exchange or internship terms around them?

title: Yuh vs neon vs a real bank: which account actually makes sense for a student salary?
body: Finally landed my first paid internship in Lausanne (5th semester, EHL) and HR told me I need a Swiss IBAN before the first salary lands. I'm weighing Yuh vs neon vs going to a physical bank, and honestly it's overwhelming. Yuh is the Swissquote + PostFinance thing, neon partners with Hypothekarbank Lenzburg — both are free, and neon even gives you a free Maestro/card combo. The catch I'm seeing: neon charges for cash deposits and some people say fintech accounts can be flagged if your salary comes from an internship that's technically a work contract. My parents keep telling me to open a 'real' bank account because internships can become full-time offers and banks look at salary history. But I don't want to pay CHF 10-15/month in fees for the next three semesters. Questions: (1) Has anyone had issues getting a salary deposited to a Yuh or neon IBAN? (2) Do fintech accounts hurt your chances with a mortgage or credit check later? (3) Is there a free tier at a traditional bank I'm missing, like a student package that stays free after graduation?

title: Quellensteuer as a student with a work permit B: am I doing my taxes twice?
body: I'm on a B permit (not C) working a 20% service job alongside my studies at Les Roches, and HR automatically withholds Quellensteuer from my paycheck every month. A friend told me that since it's my only income, I don't need to file a Swiss tax return — the withholding IS my final tax. But another friend said if your gross income crosses a certain threshold, the canton demands a full declaration and you might get a refund or owe more. The numbers confuse me: my annual gross will be around CHF 24k, plus a 13th salary that gets taxed in the same month it's paid (which feels unfair since it bumps me into a higher withholding bracket for one month). Questions: (1) Under what income threshold is Quellensteuer truly final for a B-permit student? (2) If my 13th salary spikes one month's withholding, can I get that corrected or refunded at year-end? (3) Does a partial tax return just to claim deductions (like pillar 3a) make sense if my tax is withheld at source anyway?

title: Pillar 3a at 22: locked-in savings or smart start, when I might leave Switzerland?
body: I'm 22, starting my MSc at Glion this fall, and a Swiss friend keeps pushing me to open a pillar 3a account 'now while your rate is 22'. I get the logic — deduct CHF 7,258 (2026 max) from taxable income and grow it tax-free. But here's my problem: I'm not sure I'll stay in Switzerland long-term. Everyone in my program is either going back to Dubai, Asia, or the US for hotel F&B roles. I've read that if you leave Switzerland permanently (and move to a non-EU/EFTA country), you can withdraw your 3a savings and the tax rate is usually favourable compared to EU moves — but the actual tax depends on the canton you're in when you leave. My internship income is low enough that Quellensteuer is my final tax, so a 3a deduction might not even save me much now. Questions: (1) Is 3a worth it if I can't actually deduct it (final withholding tax)? (2) Roughly what do people actually pay in withdrawal tax leaving from Vaud vs Zurich? (3) Should I split my contributions between a bank 3a and an insurance-based one, or does that only matter later?

title: Why do Swiss HR and the 13th salary make budgeting feel impossible?
body: Started my 6-month internship at a five-star in Geneva and I'm trying to build a budget, but Swiss payroll is doing my head in. First month is partial, fine. But then HR explains the 13th salary is paid half in June and half in December (which for me means the full CHF 3,400 gross just shows up in December). Meanwhile my rent is due with QR-bill that I need to pay within 30 days, my phone bill only accepts TWINT or direct debit, and my health insurance premium (about CHF 280/month for the KVG basic plan) keeps getting withdrawn early. Every finance Youtuber tells me to 'budget monthly' but my income isn't monthly — it's lumpy. Questions: (1) How do other students treat the 13th salary — savings, or normal cashflow that gets pre-spent? (2) Does anyone use budgeting apps that handle Swiss QR-bill payments and TWINT, or is a spreadsheet honestly better? (3) Should I negotiate with my landlord to split rent into smaller QR-bills, or is that weird? (4) eBill vs manual QR payment — any hidden fees either way?

title: I accidentally missed a QR-bill deadline and now there's a reminder fee — is that legal?
body: Full transparency: I'm a master's student at SHMS and I forgot about an eBill from my health insurer — the QR-bill with the orange reference number stayed 'unpaid' for 20 days past the due date. The insurer sent a reminder with a CHF 10 fee, and now I'm spiralling because I've heard Swiss companies can send a second reminder, then a 'Reto' (Betreibung/collection) that actually shows up on your credit record and can affect future apartment rental applications and permits. I already paid it, but I'm scared this will follow me. Questions: (1) Is a CHF 10 reminder fee standard and legal, or can I contest it? (2) At what point does a missed QR-bill actually escalate to a formal collection (Betreibung) — how many reminders? (3) Does a paid-with-delay bill still leave a trace on your record, or is only the formal Betreibung visible to landlords? (4) Is there a way to set up automatic payment for QR-bills so I never miss one again without paying for premium banking?

title: Regie vs private landlord: why is it almost impossible to get an apartment without a C permit or Swiss guarantor?
body: Looking for my first real apartment in Montreux after two years in student housing at Glion, and I'm hitting a wall. Every regie (property management company) asks for the same package: payslips for 3 months, an extract from the debt enforcement register, a copy of my work permit, and usually a guarantor. I have the first two, but my permit is a B and I don't have a Swiss parent to guarantee me. Some regies flat-out told me they auto-reject anyone without a C permit. A private landlord I found on anibis.ch is more relaxed but wants three months' rent in advance as a deposit in a blocked account — which I can't easily free up as a student. Questions: (1) Is the 'no C permit = rejected' policy legal, or just common practice in Vaud? (2) Do regies accept bank guarantees from Swiss institutions instead of a personal guarantor? (3) Any tips for making a B-permit application stand out — reference letter from the school, longer lease, larger deposit? (4) How do other international students actually solve this — co-renting where one person signs?

title: Finishing my diploma but my B permit is tied to my studies — do I have to leave before my internship starts?
body: This is giving me real anxiety. I'm on a student B permit issued for my studies at César Ritz, and my internship with a hotel in Zurich doesn't start until two months after my graduation date. The school said the internship is a mandatory part of the programme so it should be covered, but my permit technically expires at the end of my studies, and SEM's rules are strict about not working before the permit is updated. I've read that mandatory internships are generally allowed as long as they're required for the diploma, but my permit card's validity dates don't match my actual schedule — there's a gap. HR at the hotel says I need a valid work permit before my first day or they can't onboard me. Questions: (1) Does a mandatory internship automatically extend my student permit, or do I need to apply for a new one in advance? (2) Who applies — me directly, or does the hotel sponsor a new permit? (3) What happens during the gap month: am I allowed to stay in Switzerland on a pending application, or do I technically have to leave and re-enter? (4) Anyone been through this exact situation and can share the actual timeline of documents?

title: Missed the 3-month deadline – has anyone actually gotten backdated cover?
body:
Started at Les Roches in March. Landed, got swept up in intro week, then straight into my first practical internship, and somehow the health insurance deadline completely slipped my mind. Now my 3-month window from arrival has passed and I still don't have Swiss cover. I'm a non-EU international student, so I know I'm not exempt. A friend told me insurers can backdate coverage to your arrival date, but apparently there are limits on how far back they'll go, and I've seen different things about whether it's a hard cut-off. I don't want a gap in cover when I'm working hotel shifts, and I'm a bit worried about the canton charging a fine or premium surcharge. Has anyone here actually sorted this late?

Questions:
- How far past the 3-month deadline were you, and did the insurer backdate to your actual arrival?
- Any fines or warnings from the cantonal authority for the gap?
- Did you apply through Swisscare or a regular insurer directly, or use a broker?

title: HMO vs family doctor vs Telmed – which managed-care model do you recommend for a student?
body:
About to sign up for my compulsory Swiss health insurance and the choice of model is stressing me more than the deductible. I'm 24, so still in the young-adult premium band, but a full premium still eats a huge chunk of my student budget on top of rent in Lausanne. I get that going with a managed-care model — HMO, family doctor or Telmed — cuts the premium by roughly 15-20%, but you have to go through your GP or the phone line first before you can see a specialist. My gut says Telmed because I'm rarely sick, but I have doubts about what happens on a Sunday in a student residence with a 40-degree fever. I've been comparing on both priminfo.admin.ch and Comparis and the prices differ slightly between them, which makes me not trust either fully.

Questions:
- Is anyone on Telmed or Medgate — does it actually work in practice when you're ill at 2am?
- Is saving ~40-60 CHF/month worth the restriction for someone who mainly needs a doctor for sports injuries?
- Which model do you find works best for students doing internships abroad — does HMO still cover emergencies overseas?
- Which site gave you the more accurate premium quote, priminfo or Comparis?

title: Prämienverbilligung as a student – do international students actually qualify?
body:
I'm 22, studying at SHMS, and picking up weekend barman shifts in Leysin to keep my head above water. A Swiss colleague told me about the cantonal premium reduction (Prämienverbilligung) — basically the canton covering part of your compulsory health insurance if your income is below a threshold. That sounds almost too good to be true on a student income, but I've read that each canton sets its own income limits and you apply to the cantonal authority where you're resident. What I can't figure out is how it works for someone like me: an international, non-EU student paying CHF 300 deductible... well actually thinking of going with a higher franchise to lower my premium.

Questions:
- Do international students actually qualify for Prämienverbilligung, or is it only for Swiss and EU/EFTA residents?
- Which office do you apply to — the SVA or the health/AVS office of the canton you live in?
- Does part-time internship income count towards the threshold and could it push me out?
- Is the reduction applied retroactively to the start of the year or only from when you apply?

title: Swisscare vs a regular KVG insurer – is Swisscare actually worth it for a student?
body:
Starting at Glion this autumn and everyone — the school, the student Facebook groups, the advisors — is pushing Swisscare. But I keep reading that Swisscare is a general KVG-compliant insurer aimed at international students and short-term residents, not some special school insurance. So I did what everyone tells you to do and checked priminfo.admin.ch and Comparis, and I found regular Swiss insurers quoting noticeably cheaper premiums for the same base coverage. Now I'm stuck between doing the easy thing and paying more, or going with a regular insurer and saving ~30-50 CHF a month over four years — that's a couple of ski passes, or in my case, a lot of late-night sushi.

Questions:
- For a full 4-year degree, does Swisscare stay competitive over time or do premiums creep up vs a regular KVG policy?
- Does Swisscare actually count as your compulsory Swiss insurance, or do you still need an exemption certificate?
- Anyone had to use Swisscare for a real claim (hospital or a broken wrist)? How smooth was the process?
- Is switching from Swisscare to a regular insurer later possible without penalties?

title: EU/EFTA student – can I use my EHIC or do I really need Swiss insurance?
body:
Starting at HIM in Montreux in September and I'm an EU citizen, so I keep getting two completely different answers about health insurance. Some people say EU/EFTA students can be exempted from Swiss compulsory insurance as long as you can prove you have cover back home with the European Health Insurance Card (EHIC), and that Swisscare is basically a scam for EU students. Others — including the admissions office — say I need Swiss cover regardless, because my internship in a Swiss hotel is part of the programme and I'll be on a student permit for several years. The whole thing is making me paranoid about having a gap in cover or, worse, a problem at border control.

Questions:
- Who actually processes the exemption — the insurer, the cantonal health office, or SEM?
- Is the EHIC valid for a multi-year programme including hotel internships, or only for short stays?
- Do you still need to prove Swiss insurance (e.g. Swisscare) for the student permit application even if you're exempt from KVG?
- What happens if my home-country cover lapses mid-semester?
